blocks.prompt: The Bubbles in the Bread
blocks.text: A pizza starts with dough. Dough is just flour, water, salt, and yeast. Yeast is alive. It is a tiny living thing, too small to see. The yeast eats the sugar in the flour and burps out little bubbles of gas. The bubbles get stuck in the dough. That is what makes the dough puff up and grow. Then the pizza goes in a hot oven. The bubbles get bigger. The dough turns into soft bread with holes inside. Next time you eat a slice, look at the edge. Those little holes were bubbles made by yeast.

the sugar in the flour
they make it puff up and grow

blocks.prompt: How Flatbread and Tomatoes Became Pizza
blocks.text: Pizza did not start as pizza. It started as flatbread. People have been baking flat rounds of bread on hot stones for thousands of years, long before anyone thought to put cheese on top. The word pizza is old too. It shows up in a written agreement from a town in Italy more than a thousand years ago. The red part came much later. Tomatoes do not come from Italy at all. They grow wild in South America, and ships brought them to Europe in the 1500s. Many Europeans would not eat them. Tomatoes belong to the same plant family as some poisonous plants, so rich people grew them for show and left them alone. Poor families in Naples were hungrier than they were worried. They cooked the tomatoes, spread them on flatbread, and sold the slices on the street for very little money. That was pizza. For a long time it was food for working people, not for kings. Now it is on almost every street in the world.

meta.templateLabel: The Flatbread That Took Over the World

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A Naples oven runs near 900 degrees Fahrenheit
The bake takes 60 to 90 seconds
Water in the dough flashes into steam
Dark spots on the crust are called leoparding
Gluten is the stretchy net that traps the gas

blocks.prompt: Ninety Seconds at Nine Hundred Degrees
blocks.text: A good pizza oven is hotter than you think. A home oven tops out around 500 degrees Fahrenheit. A wood fired oven in Naples runs at about 900. At that temperature a pizza is finished in 60 to 90 seconds. You could not walk to the door and back in the time it takes to bake. Speed is the whole point. The dough hits the hot stone floor and the water inside it flashes into steam. The steam and the gas bubbles from the yeast expand all at once, so the rim swells into a puffy ring before the middle has time to dry out. That is why a Neapolitan pizza is soft and floppy in the center and airy at the edge. The heat does something else at the same time. Where the flame licks the rim, the sugars and proteins in the dough brown and blister into dark spots. Pizza makers call this leoparding, because the crust ends up spotted like a big cat. Those spots are not burned bits to scrape off. They carry most of the flavor. None of this works without gluten. When flour meets water and gets kneaded, two of its proteins link up into a stretchy net. The net is what traps the gas. Without it the dough would leak its bubbles and bake flat as a cracker.

steam from the water and gas bubbles from the yeast
they carry most of the flavor
(inference: the gas would leak out and the dough would bake flat as a cracker)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The writer who invented Pinocchio called pizza filthy looking
Millions of Italians sailed for America after 1880
Lombardi's, New York, 1905
Soldiers brought the taste home after the war
Pineapple pizza was invented in Canada

blocks.prompt: How a Poor Man's Supper Took Over the World
blocks.text: For most of its life, pizza did not travel. It belonged to Naples, and it belonged to people who did not have much. It was cheap, it was fast, and Italians from other cities looked down on it. Carlo Collodi, the writer who invented Pinocchio, watched pizza being made in Naples in the 1880s and wrote that the finished thing looked like a piece of filth. That was a normal opinion at the time. Then people started leaving. Between the 1880s and the 1920s, millions of Italians boarded ships for the United States, and a great many of them came from the south. They carried the recipe in their hands, not on paper. In 1905 a grocery in New York run by Gennaro Lombardi was licensed to sell pizza, which is usually counted as the first pizzeria in America. For the next forty years it stayed mostly where the immigrants stayed. If you did not live near an Italian neighborhood, you had probably never eaten a slice. The war changed that. American soldiers fighting in Italy in the 1940s ate pizza in the towns they passed through, liked it, and came home asking where to find it. Demand appeared in places that had no Italian neighborhood at all. In the 1950s frozen pizza arrived in grocery stores. In the 1960s delivery chains worked out how to move a hot pizza across a city in a cardboard box. Each step made pizza a little less Neapolitan and a lot more available. So the food of the Naples poor became one of the most eaten meals on the planet, and it did it by changing. Pineapple pizza was invented in Canada. Corn and mayonnaise turn up on pizzas in Japan. Purists complain. Meanwhile, in Naples, the old way never stopped: a soft, blistered, two minute pizza, made the way it was made when nobody outside the city wanted it.

6.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Flatbread That Took Over the World

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Queen Margherita visited Naples in June 1889
Historians doubt the famous thank you note
Italy had only been one country since 1861
The AVPN wrote the rules for real Neapolitan pizza in 1984
UNESCO protected the pizza maker's art in 2017

blocks.prompt: The Queen, the Legend, and Who Owns a Food
blocks.text: Every famous food has a founding story, and pizza's is one of the best known in the world. In June 1889, the story goes, King Umberto and Queen Margherita of Italy came to Naples. The queen grew bored of French court cooking and sent for a local pizza maker named Raffaele Esposito. He baked her three pizzas, and she liked the third best: red tomato, white mozzarella, green basil, the colors of the young Italian flag. He named it after her. Pizza margherita was born, and a peasant food was blessed by a queen. It is a wonderful story. Historians are not sure it is true. There is a thank you note, supposedly from the royal household, praising Esposito's pizzas, but researchers who have examined it have raised serious doubts about the handwriting and the letterhead. Pizzas topped in those three colors appear in Naples before 1889 anyway. What is certain is that by the early 1900s the legend was being repeated as fact, and the name stuck. Ask why the story survived and you learn something about how food works. Italy had only been a single country since 1861. A dish that matched the flag, invented by a poor man from Naples and praised by the queen, was a useful story for a nation still trying to convince itself it was one nation. The legend did a job. Accuracy was not the job. The care Naples takes with pizza today is not a legend. In 1984 a group of pizza makers founded an association to define what a real Neapolitan pizza is, and their rules are exact: soft wheat flour, brewer's yeast or a natural starter, dough worked by hand, no rolling pin, a center barely thicker than a coin, a wood fired oven at roughly 900 degrees Fahrenheit, sixty to ninety seconds of baking. In 2017 UNESCO went further and added the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo, the pizza maker, to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage. The thing being protected is not the recipe. It is the skill, the gesture, the knowledge passed from one pair of hands to the next. That raises an uncomfortable question. Pizza conquered the planet by refusing to obey rules. It picked up pineapple in Canada, corn in Japan, deep pans in Chicago, and folded itself in half in New York. Every one of those is a violation of the Naples standard, and every one of them is somebody's childhood. So who owns a food? The city that invented it and can prove how it should be made, or the billions of people who took it, changed it, and made it theirs? Naples would say both, as long as you do not call your version Neapolitan. That answer is more generous than it first sounds. It does not ban anything. It only asks you to be honest about what you are holding.

(it served a newly unified Italy that needed shared symbols; cite: The legend did a job. Accuracy was not the job)
(the rules guard skill and knowledge, not a formula; quote: It is the skill, the gesture, the knowledge passed from one pair of hands to the next)
(at That raises an uncomfortable question; a short sentence and a direct question pivot the reader from facts to judgment)
(it reframes a strict rule as permission rather than prohibition; earned only if you accept that naming, not cooking, is what Naples restricts)
